newsitem.title: FRANCE: Spectre of Algerian violence returns to France.
newsitem.headline: Spectre of Algerian violence returns to France.

text.p: The spectre of Algeria's brutal civil war spilling over into France has returned to haunt security officials following Tuesday's subway bomb in Paris, in which two people were killed.

Although no one has claimed responsibility for planting the bomb on a rush-hour suburban express train, and investigators are duly cautious, evidence points to Moslem fundamentalists fighting Algeria's French-backed military rulers.

The 13 kg (28lb) gas-canister bomb packed with nails and gunpowder was of exactly the type used by Algeria's Islamic Armed Group (GIA) in a wave of attacks in France last year, in which eight people died and more than 160 were injured.
"This seems to me to bear the signature of an Islamist group," said Roland Jacquard, head of the International Observatory of Terrorism.

The latest attack came less than a week after a disputed constitutional referendum in Algeria further increased President Liamine Zeroual's powers and outlawed Islamic political parties, and a week before a group of Moslem fundamentalists go on trial in Paris for their alleged roles in attacks in Morocco.

Experts say the GIA has a clear interest in spreading its war against Zeroual to France, since strict censorship and the absence of foreign media mean that daily violence by both sides in Algeria, in which more than 50,000 people have been killed since December 1992, goes virtually unreported.
It also has a potential pool of recruits among the thousands of unemployed, alienated youths of Arab origins in France's blighted urban suburbs, as last year's bombing wave showed.
Police and justice authorities eventually ended last year's campaign after killing one top suspect, arresting dozens of others and imposing a nationwide security blanket.
But police say a key suspected organiser, Ali Touchent, 39, who uses the nom de guerre Tarek, got away -- they believe via Belgium and the Netherlands.
Touchent is suspected of having recruited Arab youths in the Lyon region to carry out attacks for the GIA, including Khaled Kelkal, gunned down in a shootout with police last September.

The nature of Tuesday's rush hour attack on a crowded Metro system just in time for the evening television news and the location, on the same line where last year's campaign began at the nearby Saint-Michel station, all pointed to the GIA.

Xavier Raufer, a terrorism expert at the Paris Institute of Criminology, said the GIA's new leader had vowed in a leaflet distributed in mosques in Algiers in the last month to carry on his assassinated predecessor's war on France.

He said Antar Zouabri, 26, had taken the leadership after internecine fighting in which previous leader Djamel Zitouni, who masterminded the hijacking of an Air France plane at Algiers Airport in December 1994 and the kidnapping of seven French monks in Algeria last year, was killed.
"GIA leaflets have been circulating in the mosques of Algiers quoting Zouabri as saying he endorses completely all of Zitouni's legacy of struggle, including the battle against France," Raufer said.
A GIA statement distributed by fax in Europe quoted Zouabri as saying "France supplies all the reasons that justify our struggle against its policy."
Jacquard said signs of imminent fundamentalist actions against France had surfaced in radical Islamic publications Italy and Britain.

French officials say the Islamists maintain active support networks in Britain, Belgium, Germany and Sweden, despite efforts by Paris to convince its EU partners to crack down on Algerian Moslem fundamentalists.
